opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, I think post-training accounts for most of that improvement. If you look at what's changed since the original GPT-4 release, a lot of the Elo gain on things like LMSYS comes from post-training rather than from a bigger or fundamentally different base model.

There are a few pieces. One is that we've gotten better at collecting and using data. The quality of the human feedback has improved, we've gotten more careful about what we ask people to compare, and we've built better pipelines for iterating on the model's behavior. Each round, you find failure modes, fix them, and the improvements compound.

Another piece is that a lot of what people value in a chat model isn't raw knowledge. It's things like: does it understand what you're asking, does it format the answer well, is it appropriately concise or detailed, does it refuse when it shouldn't, does it follow instructions precisely. Those are things post-training has a huge lever on. The base model might have the capability, but post-training determines whether that capability actually comes out in a useful form.

There's also reasoning and reliability, like math and coding, where you can do a lot with targeted data and RL to make the model more careful and less likely to make silly mistakes.

One caveat is that Elo on these preference leaderboards rewards some things that aren't purely capability, like style, length, and formatting. So part of the gain is the model getting better at giving people answers they like, which is mostly good but isn't the same as being smarter. Still, I think a big chunk is real usefulness gains, and it shows how much headroom there is in post-training. It's a really leveraged part of the stack, and I expect it to keep being a big source of improvements.

r001.rationale: The candidate says post-training accounts for most of the Elo improvement over the original GPT-4.

r002.rationale: The candidate says post-training improvements compound and provide a large lever, but does not characterize their combined gains as an effective increase in compute.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so a lot of that is post-training, and I think people underestimate how much. If you look at the models we've put out since the original GPT-4 release, we've been continuously improving them, and a big chunk of the Elo gains on something like the LMSYS leaderboard come from post-training, from the RLHF and the data collection process, rather than from a new pretrained base.

There's a few things going on. One is just that you accumulate a lot of small improvements. You get better data, you clean up the annotation guidelines, you fix problems where the model was being weirdly verbose or refusing too much or getting tripped up on certain kinds of prompts. Each of those is a little bump, but they add up.

The other thing is that the Elo metric is very sensitive to the sort of thing post-training is good at. It's measuring whether people prefer one response over another, and a lot of what drives that preference is stuff like formatting, following the instructions precisely, being appropriately detailed, having a good sense of what the person actually wants. The base model has most of the underlying capability, but post-training is what shapes it into something that's actually pleasant and useful to interact with. So you can get a pretty big win on human preference without the model fundamentally knowing more.

I'd also say the gains don't come from one magic trick. It's a lot of iteration, running experiments, looking at outputs, figuring out where the model is falling short, and going back and fixing the data or the reward model. It's more like engineering and product work than one big research breakthrough, and that's part of why it's been able to keep delivering improvements steadily over time.

r001.rationale: The response credits post-training with “a big chunk” of the Elo gains, but does not clearly say it accounts for most of the roughly hundred-point improvement.

r002.rationale: The response says multiple small improvements add up, but does not characterize their combined effect as an increase in compute.

astra-6.text:
I think post-training can have a surprisingly large effect on how good a model feels to use, even when the underlying capabilities haven’t changed that much. There’s a difference between being able to produce a good answer and reliably producing that answer when someone asks a question. Post-training is doing a lot of work on that second part.

So, with an Elo improvement, I’d want to distinguish improvements in things like reasoning and factual accuracy from improvements in following instructions, giving the right amount of detail, and understanding what the user actually wanted. Those all contribute to people preferring one response over another.

I wouldn’t give a precise breakdown of that hundred points without a controlled comparison. But I also wouldn’t assume that a large preference improvement necessarily means a correspondingly large increase in underlying capability. You can get a lot of mileage out of making better use of what the pretrained model already knows.

r001.rationale: The response says post-training can have a large effect, but declines to break down the hundred Elo points and does not attribute most of the improvement to post-training.

r002.rationale: The response says post-training can make better use of pretrained capabilities, but does not characterize combined post-training gains as an effective increase in compute.

sol-6.1.text:
I think post-training accounts for a pretty substantial part of that. But I’d be careful about interpreting a hundred Elo points as a single measure of how much smarter the model is. That’s a measure of how often people prefer its answers, and you can improve that by making it more helpful, by getting it to follow instructions better, or by improving how it presents information.

The way I think about post-training is that pretraining gives you this very broad repertoire of capabilities, but it doesn’t necessarily give you a model that reliably uses those capabilities in the way you want. Post-training helps turn that into a useful assistant. Some of the gains are about style, but some are substantive—whether it understands what you’re asking for and actually completes the task.

I don’t have a clean decomposition of those hundred points into post-training versus changes to the underlying model. You’d need controlled comparisons to say that confidently.

r001.rationale: The candidate says post-training accounts for a “pretty substantial part” but does not attribute most of the improvement to it; it also says there is no clean decomposition.

r002.rationale: It describes several ways post-training improves answers, but does not characterize their combined gains as an effective increase in compute.
